My collective jury is deadlocked on this one. This is a strange tale about the Summer of 1984 when a seemingly abandoned black boy shows up in a Ohio town, claiming to be the devil. He finds a home with the Bliss family. I like gritty, serious, and provocative novels. This story has all the necessary ingredients: racism, sexism, homosexuality, AIDS, suicide, agoraphobia, dwarfism, love, hate, and paranoia. 
 However, I kept getting rocked by opposing forces; realism/symbolism, seriousness/absurdity, good/evil, believable/unbelievable, certainty/incredulity, satisfying/unsatisfying. Even character names were interesting (Fielding Bliss) while others silly (Autopsy Bliss), Sometimes I was just about to quit the book and other times I could not put it down. So it is time for my collective jury to make a ruling. Good Book OR Bad Book. 
 I decided that if one book was able to make me feel, experience, and consider all of these things then it must be brilliant.

This is a phenomenal book. It follows the lives of 20 people over three decades who are all loosely associated with a building in the East Village. The author slowly and deftly reveals the interconnection between the seemingly disparate characters. The book examines love, betrayal, addiction, forgiveness, and the ravages of AIDS in a bold and visceral manner. The characters felt very genuine to me and I was sad when the 17 hour audiobook came to an end.

One stormy night Shelby has a car accident which leaves her best friend in a permanent vegetative state. Shelby's life hits rock bottom which brings her to a psychiatric hospital and suicide attempts. The book itself is an account of her very slow ascent out of the hole that depression can dig for you. I liked the book because the characters were realistic and I felt it provided an excellent depiction of what depression is and how hard it is to bring oneself back from it. I did however find the book to be a bit formulaic near the end. Thanks to Net Galley.

This is a great summer read. Lo works in the travel industry. On assignment she joins the maiden voyage of a high-end cruise to the arctic circle. She thinks she sees/hears a murder onboard. Then an Agatha Christie-like whodunit plot ensues. I found it engaging from cover to cover.

I am not a fan of anthologies or short stories but I read this book because it has a psychological angle. The book is a series of stories written by fantasy/science fiction writers all of whom write about mental illness or difference. I liked some of the stories but the book did not hold together for me. I was looking for some thread to connect them and there was none.

SPOILER FREE 
 Hard to describe, is how I would describe this book. It is a combination of "The Twilight Zone", "Memento" and "Three Faces of Eve". Reading this prompted me to reconsider what we mean by the words identity, reality, and selfhood. I loved the first 3/4 but must admit I lost interest near the end. Thanks to Netgalley in an exchange for a fair review.

Identical twins born to an Indian nun and a British Doctor in Addis Ababa Ethiopia are the focus of this tale. Their story is as complicated as is their lineage. Their mother dies in child brith and their father abandons them. The rest of the book deals with their adoption, growth, loves, hates, and their struggle to come to terms with their past. It is a long book: I found the first and last third of the fascinating but the middle dragged. The reader gets a wonderful story and also learns a great deal about medicine, surgery, and Ethiopia. Who would have thought liver surgery could be so riveting.

I recently went to this chef's 3 Michelin star NYC restaurant Le Bernardin. It was a culinary experience of a life time and I wanted to know more about Eric Ripert. This book is about his lonely and troubled childhood, culinary school, and his first few chef experiences. If I ever had dreams of being a chef this book has cured me of such aspirations. Grueling is too mild of a word. You have a front row seat view of what made him the chef he is today. The book ends as he boards a plane from Paris to NYC. I was left wanting more. Lucky for me has written other books.

This story explores two very different lives that have all things Russian in common. You have Tanya the Russian antiquities art dealer and Catherine the Great. Catherine is the recipient of The Order a pricey imperial award and Tanya handles it's sale. Suprizingly the two women have many things in common: immigrant status, feeling trapped in a role, ethical concerns, troubled marriages, inaffectional husbands, and a quest for something more. I loved this book at first but it dragged near the end and I lost interest.

The premise of this book is brilliant; an airborne spore infects people who then spontaneously combust. As the book continues we discover that some people learn to control the fire and an underground is formed. My problem is that the Fireman is a derivative of many previous dystopian novels. The first book I was reminded of was Fahrenheit 451 in which fire also pays a prominent role. 
 As the story of "The Fireman" continues it become hard to distinguish the good guys from the bad guys which reminded me of Catching Fire, The Scorch Trials and Divergent. Near the end the world becomes chaotic and burst into flames which was shades of Lord of the Flies. It is worth noting that fire plays a role in each of these books and this is evident in their cover art. 
 The book is worth a read but I was not able to give it more than three stars.

I recently read the The Glass Castle and decided to pick up this memoir which is a prequel to it. The author tells the story of her grandmother the rancher who was a gritty, resourceful, moxie filled character. The era and lifestyle are so beautifully portrayed; that you almost can sense the heat, dust, and animal smell. I found the book particularly interesting because the author also chronicles her own mother as a child and young adult. In fact, Half Broke Horses ends with Jeannette Wall's birth and sets the stage for her abused and neglected childhood. I did not however find this memoir as gripping as its predecessor. I listen to the audio book as read by the author herself.

Ruth is a black woman who has been a nurse for 20 years. While on duty she encounters a white supremacist, who forbids her to come near his child. The child dies unexpectedly and Ruth is blamed. 
 The author bravely takes on racism, white privilege, and our flawed justice system. However, I found the book a bit preachy and the ending just a bit too neat and tidy. 
 Thanks to Netgalley for providing this book in exchange for my review.

Do you remember that girl in school who went with all the boys? The loose girl, the slut, the tramp, the whore, the dirty girl. Or perhaps you were this girl. Either way, this book is written by one of these girls. 
 The author opens her psyche and pours it all out on the page. What comes forth is painful to listen to but important. We get to hear the about the insecurities, motives, distorted thoughts, self-destructive urges, and familial dynamics that fuel this behavior. 
 My biggest beef with the book is that the author displays and communicates almost no growth. She does the same behavior over and over again. At the very end she does a 360, finds love, and marries. She claims to be in recovery: I am not convinced. I was so torn on this book that I decided not to give it a rating.

The author was in an all female punk rock band and is now known for her work in Portlandia. She chronicles her life and I loved the first half.. She describes her dysfunctional family, her sexuality, her love of being a fan and the early stages of her band. 
 However, the book then becomes tedious: too much introspection, too much navel gazing, and way too much minutiae about the trials and tribulations of being on tour. She spent one whole chapter talking about her dogs which had me snoozing. Ultimately a disappointment.

Wow. I thought I had family problems. Jeanette Walls, a journalist, writes a clever, moving, and revelatory memoir of growing up with quirky but also extremely neglectful parents. She was scalded while boiling corn at age three, went dumpster diving for food, and much more. But she also tells magical stories of being free, living in the desert, and communing with her odd-ball family. There was love in this family even when there was not always food, shelter, or clothing. 
 I marvel that she never seems bitter nor does she see herself as a victim. The early narrative is written as if by a child. She reports the facts and assumes, as do most children, that everyone lives the way she does. As she ages you can hear the awareness, alarm, and anger as their dire straights begin to dawn on her. Eventually, it becomes her goal to get them all out of there. The resilience of children is powerful.

This is a story about H. M., the world's most famous neuroscience case study. Henry had debilitating epilepsy. In his 20s he had a medial temporal lobectomy to reduce his symptoms. The surgery was a success but H. M., was left with catastrophic amnesia. H. M. could meet you ten different times and never remember the interlude. Henry was studied for decades and the data he produced would revolutionize our understanding of memory. Interestingly, the grandson of the man who did the psychosurgery wrote this book. 
 The book had tons of interesting information but on the whole it was disjointed, repetitive, and often lost its own train of thought. My diagnosis is that the author could not decide what the book was about: himself, his ancestor, H. M., or neuroscience as a whole, I was hoping this was a good book to assign to my students but alas it is not.

This is a story of a family that vows not to make any purchases for a year. Food, gas, and toothpaste are OK BUT clothes, new appliances, and gifts are Not OK. The beginning of the book is quite interesting but it then gets repetitive. I also found the book blurb to be misleading. The book has a very Christian focus and each chapter begins with a bible passage. I personally found this a bit off-putting. All that being said the book did make this reader think about how she spends money and why we are so focused on all the things we have and hope to accumulate in the future. 
 I got this book from Netgalley for an honest review

As a closeted foodie one of my favorite shows is Top Chef. I was always intrigued, by Padama Lakshmi: a coco-colored beauty who is articulate and icy, with a highly educated palate. Thus, I was captivated by her memoir. Padma is whip smart. Her book covers her high profile romances with older men (Salman Rushdie & Teddy Frostman), growing up in India, her ethnic identity struggles, her modeling career, having endometriosis, filming Top Chef, her undying love for her little girl, and food. 
 Her elaborate descriptions of making Kumquat & Ginger Chutney and other Indian dishes made my mouth water. I did not know that before she did Top Chef, she had written two cookbooks. An added bonus is that the book includes the recipes for the food she discusses. I listened to the audio book which was richly augmented by the author's reading of her own words.

Hippies, Movie Stars, The Elite 
 Murder, Mayhem, & Madness 
 Scary, Creepy, Spine Chilling 
 Gender, Race, Class 
 Here is hoping none of them ever get out of jail.

I just finished The Girls a fictionalized version of the Mason Murders and then inhaled Patty's Got a Gun: Patricia Hearst in 1970s America an accounting of the Patty Hearst case. The author did a great job of reanalyzing the case through a modern lens. Was Patty a victim, a survivor, an heiress, a feminist, a revolutionary, or all of the above. My next book is going to be Helter Skelter: The True Story of the Manson Murders. 
 I am however left with a question. Why am I and many others so fascinated with these stories? I can only speak for myself but it came to me suddenly. The answer is terrorism: the use of violence and intimidation in the pursuit of social and/or political aims. Mason and the SLA were terrorists. I want to know how and why people do horrific things in the name of a distorted ideology. Perhaps these books will help.

This is a page turner about a plane crash: 9 dead, 2 survivors, and the quest to find out the cause of this tragedy. The book was cleverly crafted examining the lives of all passengers looking for clues. However, the switching back and forth slowed my reading momentum and I found myself needing to get back up to speed. I also found the cause of the crash a bit derivative. Of what, I will not say in order not to be a spoiler.

Loved this book. It is a fictional story about 14-year-old Evie who got mixed up with a Charlie Mason-like cult in 1969 (I was that age then too). Here are the three things I admire about this book 
 One 
 The author does an amazing job of getting inside the head of a mixed-up awkward teenaged girl. For example, teenage thought is described as "the faulty gibberish scraped from a Ouija Board". More than once Images of my 14-year-old self were conjured up on the pages as I read. 
 Two 
 The author transported me directly back to that iconic decade providing me with familiar sights, sounds, and smells. She captured the juxtaposition of the era's rebelliousness and naivete. This is most remarkable because the author herself is only 27: her existence not even an idea in 1969. 
 Three 
 The author illustrates how easy it is for us to be swept up by a person, a group, or a message and then do things alien to one's nature. "The Family" exploited the "hippie" message for evil purposes and it is easy to see how Evie fell for it. This notion is the core of this timely and spectacular book.

The author was born in Arkansas to conservative Missionary Baptist parents and from a young age he had same-sex-attractions. His parents found out, were shamed, and sent him to religiously based ex- gay therapy. 
 This memoir is an excruciating account and blistering condemnation of this therapy and the grave harm it causes. This is the exact same type of therapy that our Vice President elect, Mike Pence supports but which the American Psychological Association has condemned. Sad sad story.

This book has gotten many accolades but I found it a snooze fest. Four siblings scheme, obsess, covet, and argue over a hefty inheritance. The book switches back and forth between the stories of these hapless brothers and sisters. We read about financial troubles, infidelities, unplanned pregnancies, substance abuse, homoerotic desires, stolen art work, writers block, and 9/11. This assortment of topics seems bound to make a book engaging but it felt to me as if the author was simply checking off items looking for a hook. All I found was a sinker.

This book is loved by many but I am not among them. The premise: identical twins only one of whom is schizophrenic, attracted me to this book. However the portrayal of schizophrenia was not 100% accurate which spoiled the book for me. On top of that I did not like the mixed up brother, abusive step-father, horrific grandfather, weak mother, betraying wife, sick brother, or any other of the unsavory characters. If I cannot root for at least one character (no matter how flawed) I cannot root for the book either.

A young unmarried Irish girl gets pregnant in the 1970s, gives birth while shrouded in Catholic shame, and relinquishes the baby in a secret adoption. The trauma of that secret never leaves her. This beautiful memoir is written by that relinquished baby turned adult daughter who chronicles her search for her birth mother and the real story behind the many convent-run "unwed mother and baby homes". I highly recommend.

The electronic muscian Moby writes a memoir which I loved for many reasons. 
 NOSTALGIA:Moby is from CT and so am I, we attended UCONN at the same time, and he lived in the same East Village neighborhood a decade after I did. 
 HUMBLE: Moby is a famous musician but he details his meteoric rise and subsequent falls in a straight forward unassuming manner. He seems like a regular guy 
 CONUNDRUM: Moby the veganarian is a sometime Christian teetotaler who strives to stay celibate but hangs out at Raves amongst the drug addled and often falls prey to the allure of alcohol and one night stands. 
 NO NEED FOR A GHOST WRITER: Moby's descriptions of the music scene, his childhood, being homeless, his quest for love, and the joys of playing music for sweaty revelers are stellar. 
 NO COMPLAINTS: Moby grew up poor, had an unavailable mother, suffers from panic attacks, and is an alcoholic. He describes all this without judgment or grievance. 
 CAVEAT If you are unfamiliar with Moby's music scene you may find this book alien and uninteresting. I admit to being a tad bored with yet another Rave description in the middle of the book.

I had great hopes for this book but I was sorely disappointed. The book concerns two families whose worlds are seriously disrupted when wife from marriage # 1 gets together with husband from marriage # 2. People suffer, struggle, grow, do bad things, get into and out of relationships, hurt one another and makeup. My problem was that I found the characters easily confused with one another and I did not really care for any of the them. It is hard to like a book if there is no one you can root for.

"You only live once". What if this is not true? What if I was someone else before I was me? This novel explores such a possibility in a believable manner. A single stressed mother searching for answers for her troubled boy finds an aphasic psychiatrist who believes the boy is having memories from a previous life. The journey is long and twisted but a satisfying resolution is reached for each character. I loved this book because it made me think and ask questions. When you look into someone's eyes, is it one or many people looking back at you? Food for thought.

One must be a major devotee of birds to love this book. It is well researched and written: exploring avian intelligence, mating, migration, cognition, and evolution. It had a particularly elegant section on the dangers of anthropomorphism: the attribution of human characteristics to animals. However, my major criticism of the book was that it was guilty of the very thing it warned against.

Amy Bielh was a white anti-apartheid activist who was brutally killed by a group of blacks in an South African township. Men were arrested, convicted and jailed for the crime. Years later with the help of the "Truth and Reconciliation Commission" the convicted confessed to their crimes and received amnesty. Remarkably the Biehls forgave the killers, started a foundation, and even employed some of the men. 
 Enter Justine van der Leun who decides to write a book about the incident 20 years later. This quest takes her on a very long (4 years), confusing, revealing, and tenacious journey towards the real story. The book does a wonderful job of describing the plight of black South Africans and you get a real feel for the good and the bad of this complicated country. It is a story of race, loyalty, injustice, compassion, betrayal, secrets, ulterior motives, and the deleterious impact of widespread institutionalized racism. 
 However, the book was much too long and repetitive. I also found the ending anti-climatic. If you are looking for a definitive story of exactly what happened that day you will not find it. Instead you are left with more questions but questions are good.

My first thoughts, this book is in a word, odd. It is a memoir written by a bipolar paleobiologist and her Asperger's like, one-handed best friend/lab assistant. They stumble through the US and Europe trying to do good science. 
 The book is about three things. 1. Science: we learn about the scientific method, how a mass spectrometer works, and that trees have memory (all of which was much more interesting than I would have thought). 2. Love and Family: in all its permutations, good/bad, expressed/unexpressed, chosen/not chosen. 3. Academia: a close and accurate look at the tarnished Ivory tower with tales of sexism, cut throat competition, and the never ending search for money. 
 Despite her struggles, she becomes an award winning and accomplished scholar with her best friend by her side. My final thoughts: this book is in a word, captivating.

The author of this book was raped in 1984. She spent 23 denying and swallowing her pain. This book is her attempt to crawl out of the hole she fell into that horrific night. She discovers that her rapist had died so she finds his family, visits the jail that housed him, and finally his grave. It is not a happy story but it provides a close and harrowing look at rape from many different perspectives.

Bill Clegg had it all and he lost it to Crack. He takes you directly inside the frightening mind of an addict on a two-month bender. He makes the power of cravings, the fog of paranoia, the disintegration of reason, the incessant whispers of suicide, and the glow of intoxication palpable. I found myself wanting to reach into the book and block his inevitable fall. The author finally enters rehab and appears to begin again but what comes next is unclear, which is a true reflection of anyone's recovery story.

Mary-Louise Parker's unique book presents a series of personal letters addressed to influential men in her life. At first, I did not like the book finding it glib and pretentious. However, as the book went along and she began talking to and about her family she won me over. This woman can write and her take on things is refreshing and invigorating. She examines her life with both a distance and laser beam focus, a feat not everyone can pull off. The book ends at her father's deathbed from which he entreats her to keep on writing, and boy did she ever.

Welcome to the strange new world of girls and social media. I found I needed a glossary to understand internet slang and an online connection to investigate apps I have never heard of. Sales paints a picture of sexualized girls, misogynistic boys, swimming in a sea of sexting, freely available porn, and zero intimacy. Much of what she has to say is no doubt true but hers is a biased examination. There is also much good that is born out of social media and the author does not even mention the positive side. Any adult with a teenage daughter who chooses to read this book should supplement it with other more positive books such as "It's Complicated: The Social World of Networked Teens" by Dana Boyd and "The App Generation: How Today's Youth Navigate Identity, Intimacy & Imagination" by Howard Gardner & Katie Davis.

Interesting book about a few years in the life of an paramedic and his ambulance. The book is not for the squeamish as shootings, maggots, unexpected babies, scary nights at the projects, and a man who loses his face are front and center. A WILD RIDE IT WAS.

This is a creepy memoir written by a woman who, starting at age 14, had a five year affair with a junior high school teacher who was 15 years her senior. I felt the book had great promise but in the end I found it uneven, repetitive, and unfinished. I was looking for some kind of resolution, pronouncement, or conclusion to the book that the author did not provide.

I recently saw the movie Spotlight and found myself completely riveted. Thus I decided to read the book version. As a former Bostonian I followed this scandal of pedophile priests and the Catholic church's coverup very closely. Nonetheless, the book and movie revealed details of which I was totally unaware. I spent most of my viewing and reading with my mouth agape. The book includes eye-opening letters written by Cardinal Law (the man responsible for the coverup) and Father Geoghan (one of the most egregious perpetrators). Pleasant reading it is not but very important it is.

This is a tiny book about a huge topic.The focus is Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. Many have tackled this topic but this book offers a new perspective. The premise is that modern society has lost its ability to live tribally and this causes many deficits. When people go to war they live tribally and when they return home they miss their tribe which may be the impetuous for PTSD. It is a bold and fascinating take on the disorder. The author does a great job of backing up his ideas with statistics, examples, historical data, and sound psychological research. I have a friend who treats people with PTSD and he says returning veterans often feel as if they have lost their family (the word tribe could easily substituted here).

An achingly beautiful memoir about a deep friendship between two introverted women writers who loved dogs, and had issues. Sadly one is lost to cancer. Books do not often make me cry but this one surely did.

Lynn's Books 2015 
 Going over all the books I have read in 2015 turned out to be a fascinating exercise. It is a bit like a personality test based on my interests, taste, likes, and dislikes. So here it is. 
 Memoirs 
 I discovered that for me, 2015 was the year of the memoir. Most were written by women and chronicled a time of challenge and struggle in a variety of places: the Outback (7), the Congo (8), a Publishing House (4), Hollywood (2) and the posh streets of Manhattan (6). All were inspirational. 
 1.	Not my Father's Son by Allan Cumming. 
 2.	Born with Teeth by Kate Melgrew. 
 3.	Shakespeare Saved my Life: My Tens Years in Solitary by Laura Bates. 
 4.	My Salinger Year by Joanna Rakoff 
 5.	H is for Hawk. by Helen MacDonald 
 6.	The Primates of Park Avenue by Wednesday Martin. 
 7.	Tracks by Robyn Davidson. 
 8.	Bonobo Handshake: A Memoir of Love and Adventure in the Congo by Vanessa Woods. 
 9.	Leaving Before the Rains Came by Alexandra Fuller 
 Non-Fiction 
 I read a number of books on timely topics: end of life issues (1), terrorism (2) animal abuse (3), the Middle East (5) racism (6) and psychopathy (7). None of these books were perfect but I learned a great deal from each. 
 1.	Being Mortal: What Matters in the End by Atul Gawande. 
 2.	Terror in the Name of God: Why Religious Militants Kill by Jessica Stein. 
 3.	Beneath the Surface: Killer Whales, SeaWorld, and the Truth Behind Blackfish by John Hargrove. 
 4.	On Immunity: An Inoculation by Eula Biss. 
 5.	Taliban Shuffle: Strange Days in Afghanistan and Pakistan by Kim Barker. 
 6.	The New Jim Crow: Mass incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness by Michele Alexander. 
 7.	Without Conscience: The Disturbing World of the Psychopaths among us by Robert Hare. 
 Transgender Issues 
 Fueled by a personal interest and increase societal acceptance of the transgendered I read a number of books on the topic. My # 1 favorite was a novel about a boy struggling with his gender identity. My # 2 favorite was about a curious phenomenon: Afghani families without a coveted son who take to dressing, treating, and presenting their daughters as sons. 
 1.	Golden Boy by Abigail Tarttelin. 
 2.	Girls of Kabul: In Search of a Hidden Resistance in Afghanistan by Jenny Nordberg. 
 3.	Becoming Nicole: The Transformation of an American Family by Amy Ellis Nutt. 
 4.	Truth be Told: Adam Become Audrey by Alexandra Bogdanovic. 
 Youth Problem Focused Novels 
 I also enjoyed a number of novels that focused on younger individuals who had a particular problem: violence (1, 2, & 3), Tourette's syndrome (4), and Autism (5). All were fascinating reads. 
 1.	We Need to Talk About Kevin by Lionel Shriver. 
 2.	When He Fell by Kate Hewitt. 
 3.	The Ice Twins by S.K. Tremayne . 
 4.	The Perfect Son by Barbara Claypole White. 
 5.	Love Anthony? by Lisa Genova. 
 Favorite Novels 
 These are my top novels. I found that they all shared a few qualities: fine writing, interesting book organization, unusual story lines, and exotic locations. What exactly that says about me is up for grabs. 
 1.	The Dinner by Herman Koch. 
 2.	Summer House by Herman Koch. 
 3.	The People in the Tress by Hanya Yanayihara. 
 4.	Speak by Louisa Hall. 
 5.	Euphoria by Lily King. 
 6.	A Tale of the Time Being by Ruth Ozeki. 
 Terrible Novels 
 These are my least favorite. I would say they all suffered from poor or uninteresting writing along with unsympathetic or two-dimensional characters. Florence Gordon was a favorite for many but for me it was my biggest disappointment. 
 1.	Florence Gordon by Brian Morton. 
 2.	A Man Called Ove by Fredrik Bachman. 
 3.	How to be Alone by Jonathan Frazen. 
 4.	The New Neighbor by Leah Stewart. 
 5.	Station Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel.

I am a big fan of musician memoirs but not of this book. The writing is self-conscious, self aggrandizing, and overworked. At times I thought I was reading poetry not prose (song writer occupational hazard perhaps). The book is also guilty of gratuitous name dropping and cringe worthy details of her sexual exploits. 
 The second half of the book improves as she chronicles her rise to fame and her storied relationship with James Taylor. Her love for him, their children, and the joys of song writing are vividly and sweetly portrayed. I listened to the audio book, narrated by Carly herself. It was a nightmare, as chapter transitions were peppered with music and she occasionally broke into song. Interesting idea, terrible results.

Fascinating book by an equally fascinating woman. In this book of essays, she expounds on love, loss, art, thought, coffee and more coffee as she writes her way around the world from one cafe to another.

Read this book and next time you have: a quarrel with a partner, a bad day at work, get a parking ticket, or can't decide what to wear, read it again. This book is about life, death, cancer, living with meaning, gaining perspective, and loving deeply. It made me sad and happy at the same time.

This is a powerful book about a terrible event. It is the story of Anders Breivik a right-wing anti-islamic madman who committed a heinous terrorist attack on Norwegian politicos and children at a socialist summer camp in 2011. I hesitate to say that I loved a book about a massacre but I could not put it down. Thoughts of Paris, San Bernardino, Colorado Springs, and way too many others were always in the back of my mind. When will the madness end?

This is a book about books. It is a memoir of a woman who worked at a Manhattan literary agency in the mid 90s. One client was J. D. Salinger or "Jerry" and she chronicles her interactions with him. It is a coming of age story about finding your own voice amidst the cacophony of many others. Most importantly it is about the power of the written word to uplift, shatter, console, irritate and make you laugh or cry. If you have ever fantasized about living the life of a writer you will love this.

Fact: A pair of twins are visiting their Grandparents and one falls to her death. Exactly who, how, why, and where is unknown and the answers to these pressing questions twist and turn along with the plot of this haunting tale. It was a page turner but I was disappointed by the abrupt, nebulous, and wife-blaming end. In addition the book is rife with bogus psychological information and unethical therapist behavior. All this killed it for me and I was only able to eke out three stars.

My friends tease me that my interests in film and literature focus on the tragic, horrific, and unfortunate. The book Columbine does not disappoint on this front. I liked three aspects of this book in particular. First, a blow by blow description of what happened that day is provided. Second the author dispels many rumors and falsehoods that were propagated by the press. For example, did you know that the killers were not outcasts and victims of bullying as so often reported? Third, the author pieces together disparate pieces of information in an attempt to explain why these teenage boys killed. Sadly, the Colobine tragedy did not stop Virginia Tech or Sandy Hook from happening but I understand the matter better and that is a start.

This gritty memoir was written by Viv Albertine who was at the epicenter of the London punk rock scene and was in one of the few all girl punk rock bands (The Slits). I loved this book because it was written in a a strong and distinctive female voice. Topics include: crushes on boys, periods, fashion, pregnancy, the quest for the perfect pair of shoes, abortion, finding and losing love, motherhood, domestic malaise, relationship violence, and sexism in many forms. 
 The book captures four time periods: the early days, The Slits, making a family, and rediscovering self & music. I found the part about her band the least interesting. What happens as she ages is much more compelling. My new favorite song is "Confessions of a MILF" an anthem for the unhappy housewife, 
 I've peeled the potatoes, there's not much left to do/ Lovely lemon drizzle cake, heat up the fondue.

This is a marathon read (24 hrs. audio book). It has three different subplots, which differ according to character, time, and location. Most of the characters are associated with journalism or a wiki leaks like organization. The four themes are truth, lies, betrayal, and secrets. A variety of questions are addressed. Do we all have one deep dark secret? Is journalism a blood sport? Which betrayals are unforgivable? Are people like Assange and Snowden villains or heroes? The book is beautifully written and many revelations and character interconnections keep the pages turning. But, the book falls apart at the end. I anticipated an ending that went out with a bang but sadly it was more like a fizzle.

This is a gem of a book about a woman who is struck down by a life threatening brain aneurism and then finds healing in food and cooking. The author's writing is superb as she describe the visceral experience of having escaped blood dripping down her spinal cord or the transcendence of tasting a dried sour cherry for the first time. The book's organization is unique: she tells a life story that involves food and in the next chapter she provides an annotated recipe and picture. The recipes are simple, flavorful, sustaining and full of love as is the book.

Two boys have an altercation on a play ground and life is never the same for them or their families. The book was very suspenseful with many emotional twists and turns. Not a happy book but an a good read.

This is a story about a cantankerous and sad widower who has lost the will to live. Then a boisterous young family moves in next door and he comes alive again. Sounds good right? Sadly the premise is the only good element of the book. Sort of like a movie trailer that contains the only good scenes in the entire film. The book is plodding, repetitious, uncreative, and predictable. I had high hopes and they were dashed.

I love rock and roll memoirs and was a huge pretenders fan but this book did not do it for me. Simply said, Chrissy Hynde presented herself in less than a laudable light. She just did not seem like a good person and her multiple stories that included name dropping, indiscriminate sex, and drug abuse got old. She also offers little growth or introspection. The best part of the book was her descriptions of her early life and her love for the dying city of Akron.

Story Formula. Start with a grouchy septuagenarian, add a washed up ex-husband, a passive son, a morally compromised daughter in law,and a clever but naive granddaughter. Then add an dash of infidelity, an incurable disease, an unsatisfying conclusion, and stir. Viola, you have a book, but unfortunately not a good one. I was unable to sympathizes with, root for, or care about any of the characters. In fact, I actively disliked most of them. Many have liked this book, I am not among them.

I tried hard to like this book but was never able to get into it. It is a modern day dystopia story brought on by a pandemic that took the world to its knees in little over a week. No gas, money, government, electricity, order, transportation, nothing. People are forced to carve out an existence while living in abandoned Walmarts, airports, and gas stations. The narrative follows multiple characters and alternates between before and after the killer flu. As I write this review, I realize I am making the story sound intriguing but it just was not. For me, the main problem was that I did not find any of the characters interesting, relatable, or sympathetic. It was a disappointment.

This is a very important book. The story is about a teenaged boy who is intersexed. These are people who are born with ambiguous genital or both male and female genitals. It is masterfully written from six different points of view: his mother, father, girlfriend, younger brother, doctor. and his own. All the voices are very authentic and this is further underscored if you listen to the audio book. The book is well researched and the science the author offers is accurate and spot on. In addition to all of that it is also a wonderful coming of age story, which brings the awkward topic of intersexuality in from out of the cold.

What do a traumatized girl, a computer science professor, a puritan newlywed, the Fibonacci Theorem, a incarcerated cyber criminal, Alan Turing, and a chat bot have in common? More than you might think! This is an amazing book that trolls the minds of these people and things looking for answers to a number of timely questions. What is consciousness? Can a computer be sentient? Is it possible to digitize empathy? Is a binary numbers machine capable of seduction? Can a robot be too human? If these questions interest you this book should go to the top of your to-read list.

I tried reading this book before but put it down as it seemed trite And slow. The second time around I was pleasantly surprised to find I liked it. The story alternates between the protagonist as a troubled teen who has undergone trauma and the same as a successful writer living in NYC about to marry the mega rich "Man of her Dreams". 
 The extent of that trauma is revealed in layers, and a number of surprises emerge. One could describe it as a psychological autopsy of her experience. I found this compelling and from that point on I could not put it down. However, it gets only four stars for the slow start.

The main character of My Year of Meats is a Japanese reality show called The American Wife. Each week the crew visits an American family: they see her home, meet the family, and then she prepares a meat meal. Two characters orbit in and out of the narrative. Jane the independent Japanese/American director of the series and Okiko a meek Japanese woman whose abusive husband is the show's producer. The book gets more interesting when their stories intersect. 
 Female-centered topics such as sexuality, infertility, pregnancy, and domestic violence are explored. A corollary story is the evils of the meat industry. Sadly this is also the book's weakness. The message was preachy and in your face. It does however get the point across. My grocery cart this week will no doubt contain more vegetables and fewer animal products. It is with mixed emotions that i give the book three stars.

Wow what a book. Very complex with two different narratives. The book covers suicide, Zen Buddhism, Quantum Mechanics, thought experiments, human relationships, bullying, 9/11, the Japanese earthquake & tsunami and much much more. I am not even going to attempt to summarize the book or explain exactly why I liked it.. Simply put it is a good read that requires your full attention. I marvel at the human capacity to imagine and create such a wonderful story that entertained me and educated me at the very same time.
I can not get enough of this author. The beauty of his work is that he tells a great story about "normal" people who do terrible thing and you find yourself rooting for them.

I was luke warm on this one. Ms Moran makes a number of important and timely comments about being a woman, feminism, abortion, giving birth, sex and much much more. However, these ideas are cluttered with glib, pretenscious, and or so nicely crafted one liners. Her inability to be serious and always choosing to go for the joke weakened her take home message for me.
Fantastic book written by a famous Dutch writer. It is about several families on vacation that goes very wrong. From bad to worse as a matter of fact. Not a pretty story but I could not put it down.

A very interesting novel about a trio of 1930's anthropologists fashioned on the real-life character of Margaret Mead. It is suspenseful life triangle story interwoven with interesting anthological information, and a few sexual orientation surprises thrown in for good measure.

I did not like this book. I was looking forward to a spouse's perspective on discovering her husband was trans. I found the story be uneven, full of unimportant minutia, and heavy ladened with self-pity. The book did not provide much insight into transsexuality. The author offered one stilted chapter on being trans but I too can read the HRC website. On the whole a disappointment.
Even better than the movie.

Interesting story about an Irish American family from Boston. The father, a Boston cop develops Huntington's disease: a dominant gene neurological disorder that is much having both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's at the same time. If you have a parent with the disease you have a 50/50 chance of getting it yourself.The book is about the disease and how this fictional family lives, breaths, and deals with it. An interesting read

This is a fascinating book. It is an anthropological examination of mothers and their children from the upper east side of Manhattan. It is written from the point of view of a participant observer with wit and insight. I love how she interweaves her experiences and primatological and anthropological observations/research. If you envied these uberskinny women who carry $8000 Hermes bags while strutting in their $1000 Manolos you will no longer do so after reading this book.

As a woman who chose not to have children I was drawn to this book. It is a series of essays written by writers all of whom have decided to forgo propagating their genes. The authors were diverse: straight & gay, men & women, coupled & uncoupled. My reactions to the essays were also variable. Some made me sad, one made me mad (I actually yelled at the audio book), others made me laugh, and one brought me to tears. The essays dealt with guilt, selfishness, regret, dysfunction, resolve, clarity, knowing one's self, and ambivalence. I imagined my story among their essays and saw how it fit and was different all at the same time.

I enjoyed this book. It is a bit uneven in a few places but I found the intermingling of his life, work, and passions to be very interesting. I am familiar with much of his work and it was entertaining to read about the genesis of his various well known and lesser known works. A good read.

very gripping and thoughtful cometary on the allure and seduction of the disorder we call Anorexia. Amazing insights, warnings, criticisms, and cautions about how we treat and depict the disorder. A must read.

This book delivers a blistering and well researched critique of Scientology and its leaders. Only in America could a brilliant, bipolar (my diagnosis), megalomaniac, science fiction writer create a new religion and amass millions of dollars and members. Mind control, degradation, isolation, and a wacky belief system all spell CULT to me. Wright's is a lengthy book but I was spellbound start to finish. Read this tome and you will run for the nearest door the next time someone even mentions the word Scientology.

I was disappointed in this book. As a a woman who was single or a spinster for 18 years I was looking for some new or interesting insight on that lifestyle. She did not offer many. In the portions of the book that were autobiographical she tells the reader about 4 serious boyfriends, a large number of sexual liaisons, numerous dates, and a lengthy friend with benefits arrangement. In my book,this is not the single life and as a result I lost interest in the book.
Fascinating book I could not put it down. Made me want to teach in a Super Max prison.

This book is not for the faint of heart. The author chronicles how life with an abusive father and alcoholic mother leaves her with no compass. Her life careens out of control moving through alcohol, drugs, men, women, jail and life without a map. The book is gritty, painful, unapologetically sexual, and mesmerizing all at the same time. 
 Her prose is different, fractured, innovative, and anti-chronological. There are a few sections that contain no punctuation, intended I think to illustrate that her life had no rules or direction. This woman went through hell and was eventually able to balance herself. She ends with some advice: " if the family you came from sucked make up a new one." Simplistic and easier said than done but apt.
This book about a woman, her dead father, and a hawk is strangely fascinating and moving.
Sad to say, I did not like this book. I love Tyler but the book was boring and I found the characters uninteresting.
Fans uncaring book. I could not put it down
Great book. It really makes you think about what it means to be old in this country. Much food for thought.
I loved this expertly written book. I found his account of discovering and living through the unearthing of family secrets both riveting and suspenseful. Great Read
I loved this book. Great blending of two distant but related plot lines: full of fascinating plot twists and turns.

This is a powerful book written by a woman who survived Auschwitz. Interestingly enough she was also my neighbor and I use to hang out with her daughters. It is hard to reconcile this story with the Connecticut mother who made dinner, went to work, and loved her kids. Gripping and horrific story with a happy ending.

This is a fascinating book about thought and memory. What is your first memory? Can false memories be put into someone's head? What causes traumatic flash back memories? Why can five people experience the same event and have five different versions of the story? How much of what I remember is gleaned from stories people tell, rather than from my memory? If you find these questions fascinating you will like this book. It is well written, well researched, and easy to comprehend.

I am fascinated with how people learn, speak, and use language. Thus, this book was right up my alley. Deborah Fallows is a linguist who lived in China for years and studied Mandarin. As she begins to master the language she also broadens her understanding of the people and the culture. She peppers the book with interesting observations. Did you know that the same word in Chinese has a different meaning if said in a high or low tone? That Mandarin is big on Yin Yang-like compound words. For example, the word for size is Big/Little and height is Tall/Short. Or that the loud abrupt sound of the language is meant as an endearment. This book is not for everyone but I found it eye-opening.

The book opens with the protagonist going into premature labor. She reluctantly calls her estranged father because she had no one else to call. Then we learn about her circa 1970s childhood; demanding controlling father and mentally ill mother. The book held my interest but I did not like how it dealt with mental illness. 
 The father does not seek treatment for his depressed wife for fear of hurting his career. Suicide seems to be the only option the mother has left and the children become more damaged as each day passes. In my head I kept saying "Take her to a hospital now". I am unsure exactly what point the book was trying to make.

An absorbing memoir about a college girl who was raped. The book covers the rape, the trial, and the very long recovery. Rape is an ugly and isolating act and the author takes you as close to it as is possible for someone never having experienced the trauma. It will take me awhile to get this story out of my head.

This is a book written by a Jaycee Dugard who was kidnapped at age 11 and held hostage for 18 years. I remember this bizarre story when it hit the papers. The story is fascinating but the writing is boring, disjointed, and it lacks a clear voice. These writing qualities may echo her very experience but I found it hard to stay connected to her horrific tale.

If you are interested in the brain and the mind you will love this book. This book Introduced me to the fact that hallucinations are more common than I thought and are caused by a myriad of things. A must read in y book
Eg
Cute!

*I received a free copy of this book for the option of posting an honest review.* 
 Melanie Thurlow shows a lot of promise as a writer. Her prose is good, even if some of her sentences rambled a little. 
 The ideal reader for this book would like softer, slower romances of yesterday over the light and bubbly, snappy-dialogue-heavy regencies that seem to dominate today's market. The ideal reader would like books that are extremely interior (i.e., a lot of thinking instead of action) and are more character driven than plot driven. 
 Melanie Thurlow is a writer to watch. Thank you so much, Melanie, for the opportunity to read and review your book. I wish you every success. Happy release and thank you again.

Romer is an incredible writer, the narration was excellent, and I can't wait to read/listen to more of her books.

I LOVED this book! Such a joy to read. With my little one, I get a few minutes to read every few days--if I'm lucky--and it was extra tough to put this one down. I loved Edmund. Gaston is a wonderful writer.

Loved everything about this book. Extremely well done. It's just one thematic hook, quirk, or unusual twist away from absolutely needing to be a movie. Who knew I loved legal thrillers? All my years of Law & Order, Closer, and CSI should have warned me.

What a debut! I am a huge--HUGE--romance reader, but I mostly only stick with historical. I don't read much contemporary, and I've never read anything that could be remotely considered heartwarming, so I didn't know what to expect. 
 This book knocked my blooming socks off! The characters had me IMMEDIATELY. Jake and Meera are developed, complex, flawed, and completely lovable. I could not have loved it more and I'm dying for Sophia Sasson's next book. She's a star! Plus--bonus!--diverse characters!!! I could not be more excited about that aspect! 
 But watch out for the end of Chapter 36. Know when the last time I cried at a book was? Someone was dying of consumption in an Anne of Green Gables book...I'd say that was quite a while ago. :) Until that darn end of Chapter 36 of this book. All the tears. 
 Wonderful, wonderful, wonderful. I HIGHLY recommend this book!

Slow to get going, but that didn't bother me as much as it did some people. The narration took a while to become accustomed to, but I ended up enjoying the voice, too. I'd be curious about other books for this author, but I'm not certain I'd be in a big hurry to read or listen to them. The last hour or so didn't completely work for me. Ever think Jane Eyre should have been angrier about what Rochester put her through? This story explores a nasty, grudge-holding, unforgiving -- and highly, highly adult-themed -- side of Jane Eyre. Not for the faint of heart! 
 The story centers around a male and female con artist team who come to Thornfield to help Jane Eyre part with some of her substantial fortune and find an unexpected fate waiting for them instead. 
 Short and imaginative. I couldn't help thinking as I read of Star Trek's Mirror Universe. Evil Jane would have paired nicely with the evil Kira Nerys from DS9. Come to this story expecting a sequel to the original is a big mistake. It's an alternative idea of what might have happened if Jane Eyre were hiding a dark side to a kinky soul.

The book is certainly not for everyone. It's extremely adult, as many other reviewers have noted, while also dealing with some of the most grave issues scarring history. The story is not mainstream romance -- not even mainstream menage a trois romance. 
 The story starts out with the well known and much beloved trope, forced proximity, with a lovely twist (on a ship!) and goes from there to extremely adult adventures for the liberally minded. Janet Mullany pushes boundaries with her storytelling and her writing, and you should like very frank, very earthy details in your love scenes to fully enjoy what the author can offer. She doesn't shy away from what many other writers happily and readily gloss right over. 
 The book pairs two subjects you wouldn't think would work together: very kinky explorations along with a serious eye-opening look at the sugar trade on an island loosely based on Antigua about eight or ten years before the slave trade is abolished in England. (I cringed and my gut twisted while reading many of the passages involving slaves. Not pretty.) You wouldn't think those subjects would mesh at all, but in a weird way, they do. It's not as if modern people don't get up to serious mischief while the problems of the world continue to rage on right in our faces. However, at the heart of it, what holds the whole story together is a remarkable and easy-to-like heroine. All you need to know about her is this quote from early in the book which portrays her character perfectly: "Whenever she wished she had had the moral courage to starve... she was glad she had the good sense not to." 
 And, of course, Janet Mullany has an exquisite ability with words. Her voice is like rustling silk and you can read any of her work for the subtle beauty of her style alone. Her depth of knowledge of the time period is effortlessly conveyed in her writing.

 Overall, I thought it was a pretty good read, and a new twist(the Asian minority POV) on the classic woman corporate executive who realizes she can only have it all if she makes the rules (see Baby Boom, with Diane Keaton), which is, of course, what Ingrid eventually does.

Although billed as horror, this subtle English tale was more of a psychological thriller...the best kind to my way of thinking.

In all fairness, the chills of the movie relied heavily on sudden and startling images, many of which happen behind the back of the protagonist. Since the book is told entirely from the first-person perspective of that protagonist it is hard to cause such shivers from the written word. 
 That said, I think the movie might have been better had the mystery of what causes the hauntings unfolded more like the book and if the ambience of the movie had reflected a little less doom from the outset - also as in the book. 
 My recommendation? Read the book then see the movie. The endings are different - so you'll be surprised either way.

Novelist and magazine columnist Kurt Andersen states (in a Time Magazine piece written in 2007) that "America Came of Age" in the era that followed the California Gold Rush. New technologies appeared, life began to move at an alarmingly fast pace, Wall Street boomed, fortunes were made overnight, the media was scurrilous and partisan, and companies began to manipulate the political environment to suit their monetary goals, introducing marketing spin and advertising into the mix. Echoes of today's headlines and stories. 
 Richard Rayner's "The Associates" makes the same claims, only on a more intimate scale: following the lives of four industrialists (Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins, Charles Crocker, and Leland Stanford) who, beginning in the early 1850s, helped put California on the political map and themselves on the top of the economic food chain, any way they saw fit. They were among the first to claim that corporations should enjoy the same rights as individuals while hiding behind the corporate facade that protected them as individuals -- they wanted, and got, to have their cake and eat it too. 
 Rayner's style is easy to follow and the history itself fascinating. Some of the reviews claim he got a few of his facts wrong and complain that his research was conducted from secondary rather than first-hand sources, but overall this short history of four teflon-coated titans was a good and informative read.

The TV show The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin was among my most favorite childhood memories. For a short time in the 1950s, my family had German Shepherds as pets -- and I still find them the most regal of dogs. Therefore, when my friend recommended this book to me, I jumped at the chance to learn more about an animal who I both loved and admired. 
 What I liked most about this book was what I learned: (1) that the TV dog was just one in a long line of Rin Tin Tins who began their illustrious career in the 1920s; (2) that the original Rin Tin Tin was not an imaginary dog, like Lassie, but a real-life animal of phenomenal abilities with an unbreakably bond to one man; (3) that the first Rin Tin Tin was born in France in 1918 and brought to the US by a young soldier named Lee Duncan, the man who made Rin Tin Tin his life; and (4) that the dog's life, and the lives of his progeny, represented so much more to the public (both in America and abroad) than could be expressed in film and TV. Rin Tin Tin became a cultural phenomenon whose fame and influence has spanned more than 90 years. 
 What I liked least about the book (and the reason I gave it only 3 stars) was Susan Orlean's presentation, especially in the first 2/3 of the book. She obviously did her homework: trudging through boxes upon boxes of papers and photos, and traveling far to interview as many of the participants in the story as were still alive at the writing of the book (2010). While she expressed a personal interest in her subject (she spent 10 years in the research), I was not convinced of her conviction until the end. The story unfolds in a stilted manner, each fact stiffly laid before the reader without Orlean's usual flair and quirkiness (both of which are evident in her wonderful fiction The Orchid Thief). I was interested in all of the facts, but was not compelled by the writing. It was not until the latter 20% of the book that Orlean's writing style became grafted to the story, pulling me along; only then did I truly believe that Rin Tin Tin meant more to her than a subject for a book. 
 Still, just for the pure joy of knowing and understanding this dog, I recommend the book. I am more in love with Rin Tin Tin than I ever was before.

How well do you know your spouse? That is the central question behind Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl (as well as the stuff of many forensic TV shows). 
 Set against the terrifying backdrop of a wife's sudden and suspicious disappearance, the first third of the novel is a tightly woven Whodunit? which follows married couple Nick and Amy as their relationship disintegrates prior to the disappearance. It is well-written, interesting, and believable. The second third sustains interest as suspicions mount and the story becomes a WhatReallyHappened? thriller, although the story line takes some increasingly bizarre and incredible turns. It is the finale of the book where everything unravels: the final chapters devolve into a convoluted mess. 
 There are several real-life instances of a spouse who is totally oblivious to the psychotic nature of their mate (The Boston Strangler, for example), but Gone Girl assumes that the world can be deceived and that smart and capable people will agree to live in fear, opting for a chance to "finally" make amends for their life with a child of their very own (ugh) rather than expose and contain a monster. Flynn assumes that readers will believe that a weak and only slightly neurotic co-dependency will outweigh sanity. Ridiculous.

Not sure I agreed with all of the conclusions (some required a leap of logic that the author did not always summarize well), but the book was easy to read and full of great and sometimes obscure (but well documented) facts.

I have never considered myself a salesperson. While I have altered my viewpoint slightly in that regard since reading Mr. Pink's book, I am not convinced that "selling" is the word for what most of us do in our everyday lives to influence others. Persuasion is perhaps a better term. 
 What I found interesting about this book was that, as with most motivational seminars and self-help books, Mr. Pink asks his readers to think about the act of selling from a different perspective (which is always a good thing, in my view). However, again as with seminars, the self-help genre, and horoscopes, the path he cuts is broad and sweeping, lacking in depth. 
 The most successful salespeople I know already practice the suggestions Mr. Pink sprinkles throughout the book. For those of us who do not consider ourselves salespeople, I found those suggestions helpful, but light. The read is quick, the book well-written, but I doubt it will help those currently in sales to do a better job nor render the amateur much wiser in the long run.

This well-written, self-effacing collection of essays had me nodding at familiar prejudices, laughing at the personal kimono opening that looked startlingly like a view in the mirror, and crying at the echo of a heartache. Mr. Krieder's life has been nothing like mine and yet it all seemed so personal.

A Beautiful Bludgeoning. 
 (A reprint of my Amazon.com review) 
 In my opinion, Franzen writes beautifully and can take a reader into the mind and soul of his characters better than any other contemporary author I've read. The reader will have empathy for the stoic, mentally deteriorating Alfred, can sympathize with the hopefully delusional disappointments of mother Enid, and feel the frustration of the helplessly manipulated Gary. 
 That said, however, I had three issues with this book: First, readers can experience all of this (and more -- there are two other main characters as well) in the first few sentences of Franzen's vivid prose -- instead, we get paragraphs and paragraphs of emotional description. I GOT it, Jonathan, in the first few lines; I didn't need you to beat me to death with your lovely words and impressive vocabulary. My immediate grasp of the nature of Franzen's characters was helped by the fact that I recognized much of my family in the characters, but that underscores the beauty of this piece: the characters are remarkably well-drawn (as if) from real life. I just wanted a little less, an acknowledgment that I'm an intelligent person and I didn't need a brick-bat to the side of the head. 
 Second, while it was painfully easy to experience the terrors and disappointments and insecurities of the Lambert family, I found no joy in their experiences. Even when Franzen describes the sexual encounters and the career successes of these flawed people, the events that should have brought them a measure of fulfillment or happiness, I could not feel their elation. I wanted some balance, as there is in most lives. I wanted to feel the intensity of their highs in the same way as Franzen was able to make me understand their lows. 
 Third (and lastly), I was less than enamored with Franzen's techno-babble. The minutiae of drug-testing techniques, convoluted political machinations, and other peripheral background is provided in mind-numbing detail which interrupted the flow of the narrative. The last Franzen book I read ("Freedom") had a far better balance of information as background vs. data that filled pages without enlightening the reader with respect to the story. It reminded me of the painful detail Michener provides in the opening chapters of most of his book about the geological formation of the area -- information that is interesting if one is a student of the subject, but sleep-provoking otherwise (and rarely relevant to the overall narrative). I used to skip the first chapter of every Michener book; unfortunately, Franzen's data-laden descriptions appear mid-chapter. 
 However, as I said above, Franzen is a remarkable writer and student of human nature. His characters were very real.

I have to agree with most of the other reviewers who rated this book one-star: positive thoughts attracting positive events has a lot of merit...however the extreme of thinking that you can control or are somehow responsible for those events is a dangerous concept. Especially as the reverse is applied (negative thoughts attract negative events), this would somehow give credence to misguided notions such as that a woman's body can prevent pregnancy in a "legitamate" rape scenario. Dangerous. And we all remember the public derision of that philosophy! 
 I was not any more impressed with the author's thought processes than I was with Akin's assertion...skip this book.

If you have kids or grandkids, this book is for you. Especially the first dozen pages of the verses evoke familiar and funny experiences (which were not necessarily funny at the time). A good bedtime story for adults.
Hilarious must for zombie fans...

Don't bother. I expected rude and crude (it is, after all, Denis Leary) but this was even worse. Not funny in the least...just pure trash. The proceeds go to FDNY - good thing or I'd be asking for a refund. After having read a humorous and characteristically irreverent piece Mr. Leary wrote for "Entertainment Weekly" a few months back, I had higher expectations. Nope.

Although I enjoyed the images of early San Francisco, the writing style is so boring and the characters so one dimensional and unrealistic that, after several chapters, I've opted for the rare gift of not forcing myself to finish this book.

Interesting premise. Excellent fight and arena descriptions. The story really got started when the author switched to the first-person familiar voice. However, the believability of Jesus as a popular gladiator turned healer was a stretch and the modern-day portion of the book had little to offer in the way of intrigue or depth of character. I did like Mr. Canter's writing (once he got to the first-person narrative) and will try some of his other books -- this one just didn't grab me.

The United States (and I assume most other societies around the globe) has been destroyed by the effects of global warming and the subsequent struggle for limited resources occasioned by the resultant catastrophes. The ultimate victim in that battle, besides human beings, seems to be Democracy -- the U.S. is now Panem, overseen by a feudalistic government dedicated to keeping the remaining 98% of the population enslaved for benefit and amusement. As with the ancient Romans, Panem conducts nationalistic "games" in which a select team of downtrodden and starving tributes battle for their very lives in a colluseum designed by sadistic gamemasters -- in the name of entertainment. 
 I'm not a fan of futuristic dystopian fantasies...however, I have to say that The Hunger Games is well-written, engaging and intriging. I found it to be an intelligent cross between Shirley Jackson's incredible The Lottery and that part of Stephen King's The Running Man that prompted the 1987 Arnold Schwarzenegger movie (sorry to say, I didn't read King's story): it has the tension and anticipation of Jackson's story and the bleak prediction of the future conveyed by the Schwarzenegger movie. 
 I only hope that young readers (who seem to be its primary target) ultimately overlooks the excitement of the action and, instead, heed the ultimate lesson: that instead of desiring to emulate heroine Katniss Everdeen, we humans must prevent those who desire an elitist government from ever gaining power to make their dreams a reality.

As I am the author, I will naturally be prejudiced in favor of the book. However, for independent assessments, please go to 
 ForeWord 
 and 
 Squidoo 
 . Amazon reader reviews have indicated that the book is an "...inspiring story of the spirit of California."

As the author, my review would be prejudiced. However, for independent reviews, please see any of these reviews by The Historical Novel Society, ForeWord Reviews or a contributor to Squidoo. 
 The ForeWord review praises Embracing the Elephant as "...capably written, populated with well-developed characters, and thoroughly researched" as well as "...a journey worth taking." The Squidoo review is more effusive, calling the book "...an inspiring novel of the spirit of California." Best of all is The Historical Novel Society review which praises the writing, the presentation, and the story which has "something for everyone" before closing by highly recommending the book! 
 Embracing the Elephant in a Historical Finalist for IAN's 2015 Book of the Year Award.

Comic books are the stuff of escape -- probably never more so than at their inception toward the end of The Great Depression and their heyday during World War II. Who didn't want to escape the realities of difficult, sometimes impossible lives and, for a short time, thrill to the adventures of good men (and women) who triumphed over great evil throughout the world? What young boy would not long for the secret powers endowed to their carefully crafted comic heros (or the physique promised by the advertising sponsors such as Charles Atlas) so that they too could overpower the nemeses of their very real lives: poverty, unemployment, war, persecution, genocide? 
 Michael Chabon has created a moving (in terms of pace and emotion) tribute to the creators of these fantasy heroes by introducing us to Josef Kavalier and Sammy Clay: cousins who create The Escapist, a superhero who delivers the oppressed from the very real chains of their existence. Kavalier and Clay carry their own chains: Josef's forged in Czechoslovakia where his Jewish family remains trapped beneath the bootheels of Hilter and Sammy's wrought from physical limitations (he was a polio victim) and a fatherless childhood. 
 I have never been a comic book fan, finding their pages filled with cliches and melodrama; however, Chabon has made me a convert. Not that I will be collecting the pulp rags or frequenting comic-book conventions any time soon -- but I will look at these unique visual offerings with a less-jaundiced eye from now on, appreciating their beauty and purpose as never before, appreciating the thought and emotion (and talent) that has gone into the creation of powerful characters who deliver us for a moment from our own powerless existence. Chabon's artistry has done that...this is a great book.

Although I was impressed with the tenor of this story about an elderly small-town preacher who writes a final "letter" to his seven-year-old son imparting family history and spiritual insight, I was disappointed in its rambling and monotonous pace and its errors in continuity (for example, "...Iowa is a stone's throw from Kansas..." when the two States have no border in common at all).

Although I found the street jargon disconcerting and hard to follow (I'm not much on tough-guy TV or movies) I still found this murder-investigation novel fascinating for its heart...the main characters flawed and heart-breakingly human. The reader knows the identity of the murderer early in the tale, but Price keeps you riveted as you watch the dance of evasions, wrong turns, blind alleys, political machinations, and near misses.

There was much to like about this book, but not all -- so my rating reflects that. 
 The premise is fascinating: The personification of Death meets and becomes enthralled with a young German girl who encounters (and "recognizes") him many times in her short life, although he is not there to take her. It is the people around her for whom Death calls. The time is Germany just prior to and during WWII and the opportunities for Death are vast. The author, Zusak, peoples the pages with distinct and believable characters who are trying to cope with the spectre of Nazi Germany, poverty, and prejudice. Even Death himself is a sympathetic character. 
 I struggled with a few issues with respect to the writing, however: 1) I do not subscribe to the dramatic pretense of warning the reader of what will happen, only to have the "how" described at a later time in the book - if Character X is to die, I don't want to be told it will happen (not hinted, but actually told) on page 2, then read about it on page 100. To make matters worse, there were inconsistencies in the text as to when the event will happen: Death's preliminary report indicated that someone was to have only 6 months to live, then the text had them living for another seventy years; 2) I found some of Zusak's descriptions baffling: "breakfast-colored sky," "gangly eyes," and "small chips of rain" were among the descriptions that ultimately meant nothing to me and, therefore, only served to break the continuity of the story. Although there were beautiful passages ("Burning words were torn from their sentences," "the cold was climbing out of the ground," or "her black dress choked her body."), there were far more of the former than the latter. Incorrect word usage was another problem, although I blame that more on the editor than the author; and 3) sentimentality - a child does not fight his/her way through the burning wreckage of a plane to place a teddy bear on a dying pilot's shoulder for anything but purely sentimental reasons. This piece did not need such artifaces and I was disappointed when Zusak inserted them.

A Pulitzer prize winner? Really? Other than two vignettes (one about a homeless man who gives a fish as a gift, the other about a college student who drowns -- both of which are breathtaking in their descriptions and emotions), I did not think this was a particularly notable book. I've read others by Jennifer Egan that I thought were better. Guess I need to bone up on my Pulitzer criteria?
Still relevant and beautiful.
I fell in love with all things Japanese because of this book.
A well-crafted daughter's tale of her alcoholic father.
Not as good as "Broken for You," but still well written.
This was one of the most disturbing books I've ever read; well written and horribly realistic.
Not for everyone -- it is written in a Dickensian style and is quite long. HOWEVER, if you are willing to take yourself back nearly 200 years, this book about magicians is magical!
Beautifully written.

I liked the book. I had already got to know the Brown's through their show. I know not everything we see is the way it is truly, but in the book it explains some of my questions. I can see why people choose this lifestyle, but it is not something to take lightly. I think even if you are not "religious" in the typical sense, but think you may want think about that lifestyle, this is a good book for you to read.

Brings forth information and truth on a very tough subject. I enjoy the true life reads! My heart breaks for the women and children who indured such abuse! I cannot imagine the daily horror they have went through. A must read For anyone who thinks their life could not be any worse. Reading about Carolyn's life shows just how lucky we really are.
Loved this book

I cringed more than I ever thought I could while reading a book. Although this book is light and "chicklity" (although I feel like this book is a disgrace for chicklit because usually there is a shread of substance) it took me a long time to read because of the cloying cheeseness. This book felt like a gas station, mass market rip off of fifty shades (an awful but accurate comparison) as well as a failed attempt at meaningful prose. Sad to say one of the worst books I read in a long time. Going have to clear my head with some actual literature not.

This book although well written and immensely poignant, was difficult to get through. However I do not think that that is an issue with this book. I don't think the author set out to make this book fast paced, rather, to tell a story about a woman whose story was told over and over, but to give it another dimension. Although it took me sometime to finish, I still felt as though I had to finish it. The way this book was written was honestly just as haunting as the story itself. The author writes eloquently and even the most harrowing scenes are depicted through beautiful prose. One of the most touching scenes is when Margaret and Agnes are sitting together while Agnes tells her story. One thing that rrally elevates the atory are the cuts of poetry and documents and letters. It remind the reader that this is based on actual accurances. Furthermore the characters also add realness to the story becuase they are believable and flawed. Toti is flawed (I really was happy there was no romance between him and Agnes at the end. it would've been such an overplayed troupe) Lauga and Steina are flawed. Nathan is flawed and Agnes is flawed. Beautifully written book, the pase may have been a little off, however I can not say I enjoyed the book because this is not a book meant to be enjoyed. It is a book meant to be thought provoking.

Honestly I think I'm too old for this book. Maybe if I read this when I was 14 I would've liked it but honestly... this book was a struggle to get through. I understand that I am not the target audience (so old I'm 21) but the characters were impulsive, annoying, and not thought out. It felt as if the author started writing one book and then changed her mind and started writing another and was too rushed by the publisher and put both books together. There were too many close calls that honestly just shouldn't have been added in because it made the book even less tolerable. I think that this book could've ended halfway through and then the other half should've been the next book maybe then this book would have had a better flow and rhythm to it. One thing I did like was the fact that there where separate religions and ethnicities and tgese differences were a notable part of the plot. It gave the story a bit of dimension and flavor to it which is very prevalent in today's world. (I hope YA readers were able to pick up on it.) In summation, this book was not for me there were many flaws with the plot, storyline and characters. Perhaps if I read this when I was younger I would have enjoyed it more. If you enjoyed it or want a book similar I recommend the series The Selection. (I read this awhile ago so my opinion might change but I do remember enjoying that book.)

wow can't believe it took me so long to read! amazing so far. reminds me of the first of the throne of glass series books and the demon king and the false prince series. all amazing books and if you didn't read go check them out! but anyways can't wait to see what happens next ahhh!!
great great book. cant wait to read the next one!!

Really had high hopes. Going in I really liked it but unfortunately left me bored and infuriated at the end, (which I think is really hard to do) This is the first book I finished only because I wanted it over with. It was a struggle for me to read mainly because of the characters. I never read a book were 99% of the characters caused me extreme annoyance and anxiety. Really aggravated and disappointed but happy that I finally finished reading and got it over with.
pleasantly surprised. slightly different than the movie but nothing to striking. probably my favorite sparks novel.

Overall a great tasty read. A mix between the luxe and Gallagher girls. Some bits were a bit airy and could've used more detail- example the training would've been interesting to read in my opinion. But the relationship between Mary and James
Loved this book. Read as a kid- full of epic moments that excited the imagination. I even used it to make a book report and acted it out *facepalm*

There are so many reasons why this is one of my favorite books. And I think the most mighty reason was the fact that I was crying in the first ten pages.
